research.note: Authoring metadata only. Nothing in this file reaches the player as words: titles, citations and notes are for authors, reviewers and tests.

frames: Every position is in the local frame of a room of the host building (src/urban_tableaux.rs, RoomFrame): origin at the centre of the room's floor cells at its walk surface (a room whose floor has burned out takes the XZ bounds of its own modules and its storey elevation), +Y up; a room tagged yard (and not street) faces its yard: its +Z points out of the back of the building, otherwise the building's axes (+Z toward the street facade). rest: room = y above the room's walk surface; terrain = y above the terrain at the piece; terrain_mean = y above the mean terrain under the piece's footprint; terrain_slope = as terrain_mean, the piece tilted to the terrain's slope along and across it. on = the module the piece rests on or hangs from: when it fails, the piece (and any light or smoke on it) is gone with it. of = a light, smoke or sound source positioned in a piece's own mesh frame. body: none (no collision), static (collision proxies from the source geometry), scatter (a light pushable prop of the scatter system). Yaws are degrees about +Y in the room frame.

tableaux.title: The low window: a cellar embrasure with the autumn wreck on its line of fire, and the cellar behind it

provenance.event_date_or_window: 1942-09/1942-10 (Soviet anti-tank guns in cellars against German armour); 1943-01-20/1943-01-31 (German machine guns in basement embrasures)
provenance.place_envelope: Any shelled or burned brick building of the Stalingrad city centre with a semi-basement on its street front

sources.citation: Max Plakolb, Luftwaffe liaison officer with 24th Panzer Division, September 1942, OeStA-KA B/1540, quoted in Beevor, Stalingrad (1998), ch. 10, p. 149: 'anti-tank guns concealed in the cellars make it very hard going for our advancing tanks.'
sources.framing: Contemporary German report reached through Beevor; access copy of the book; cite the printed edition.

sources.citation: Pavlov's House garrison arrangements: narrow embrasures made in windows and walls, approaches mined, wire around the house (ru.wikipedia citing Gurkin 1963); Beevor ch. 12: defenders met tanks from the cellar and the top floor.
sources.framing: Soviet-era account of a later-mythologised episode; physical arrangements only; no replica or name of the building.

sources.citation: Capt. L. P. Morozov and Capt. I. Z. Bukharov, 38th Motor Rifle Brigade, Historical Commission interviews 1943, in Hellbeck, Stalingrad: The City That Defeated the Third Reich (2015), 'The Capture of Field Marshal Paulus': German heavy machine guns in the basements, embrasures cut in the walls, 'You couldn't see any of it from outside' (29-30 January 1943).
sources.framing: Near-contemporary Soviet commission interview in edited translation; access copy.

documented_relationships: Both sides turned semi-basement windows and wall breaches into gun ports (Plakolb; Gurkin; Morozov).
German armour advancing into the centre in September 1942 was stopped by guns firing from cellars (Plakolb).
In the last days German machine guns fired from basement embrasures that could not be seen from the street (Morozov).
inferred_geometry_and_props: Both layers at one building and one window.
The wreck's type (a German medium tank, the reviewed battlefield Pz III wreck) and its position on the slot's line of fire.
The slot narrowed with loose brick and a sandbag, and the number of spent cases.
The wire's line along the pavement and where it is cut.
The wreck's scale: the source model measures about 1.39 times a Pz III hull (8.1 x 3.3 x 4.0 m against 5.56 x 2.50 x 2.95 m); it is placed at 0.72.

The cellar behind the slot (built since cellars open, 29 September 2026): the slot lies 1.9-2.35 m above this block's cellar floor, so a firing step of loose brick stands under it; the greatcoat folded on the step (R2's "brick bench"), the spent cases on the floor below it and the ammunition box with a blank lid beside it.

The September gun in the far corner: a 45 mm 53-K from its published dimensions (as the live guns of at_guns), its right wheel gone, its shield holed, shoved aside with its trails closed; how a 560 kg gun came to be in a cellar is not shown.

host.choice: R2's alternative host (an apartment block with a semi-basement): a burned five-storey block 56 m from the spawn whose street front faces the tram street and, beyond it, the open square, so the only semi-basement window left clear of the entrance steps (bay 9) has a sightline of over 100 m. No merchant house with a cellar faces open ground near the spawn. The slot fires 14 degrees off square, the wreck 36 m out in the open square: a fallen trunk at the square's edge and a boulder in the square (district dressing) stand clear of the line.

tableaux.title: The red cross over the cellar stair, and the cellar below it

provenance.place_envelope: The Stalingrad city centre (southern pocket); not the factory district (a1_factory_cellar_ward is a separate event)

sources.citation: Paulus radio report, 24 January 1943: '18,000 wounded without the slightest aid of bandages and medicines' (Adam and Ruhle 2015, p. 193).
sources.framing: Contemporary signal quoted through a secondary summary; the figure is never encoded.

sources.citation: Beevor, Stalingrad (1998), ch. 22: about 20,000 wounded in the cellars of the ruins; the theatre cellars 'with no light and no sanitation' (Dr Hubert Haidinger, 1992); a dressing station under the NKVD building with 'a red-cross flag outside the entrance' and a field-hospital gas lamp (Hans Dibold, Arzt in Stalingrad, 1949, pp. 24-25); piles of frozen corpses outside the Tsaritsa tunnels (Achleitner).
sources.framing: Retrospective German medical accounts synthesised by Beevor; access copy.

sources.citation: Beevor, Stalingrad (1998), ch. 21: limbs bound with paper for want of plaster (Dr Guenther Diez); the wounded who could not be moved left behind with a doctor and an orderly.
sources.framing: Access copy.

sources.citation: Morozov, Burmakov, Yegorov and Duka, 38th Motor Rifle Brigade, Historical Commission interviews 1943: German hospitals in the candy-factory and Univermag basements; a basement lit by car batteries and headlights; 28-30 January 1943.
sources.framing: Near-contemporary Soviet commission interviews in edited translation; access copy.

sources.citation: Beevor, Stalingrad (1998), ch. 20: frozen corpses left by a field hospital 'because the ground was frozen too hard to bury them' (Morzik, p. 188).
sources.framing: Access copy.

documented_relationships: In the last fortnight the cellars of the ruined centre were German dressing stations and hospitals, marked by a red-cross flag (Dibold).
They were lit by improvised oil lamps, a gas lamp or car headlamps on batteries (Achleitner, Dibold, Duka).
The dead were left outside because the frozen ground could not be dug (Morzik, Achleitner).
inferred_geometry_and_props: The building type, and that the station used the back door of the stair hall that leads to its cellar stair.
The pole for the cloth and where it stands, visible through the yard gate from the tram street.
The blanket in the doorway, hooked aside at one corner.
The number of the dead (four: an authoring choice, never a count), their covers, and that one has lost his boots.

The dressing station in the cellar (built since cellars open, 29 September 2026): its two rooms off the stair hall, the door off its hinges on two trestles as a table, the pressure lamp on it (the only strong light), rolled paper bandages and mess tins on it, a bucket under it; a pair of vehicle headlamps wired to a battery on a crate, aimed at the table (Duka); straw and blankets in rows along the walls; four figures under blankets, still (whether they are alive is left unresolved); two tins with wicks, and one at the foot of the stair, whose glow is what the stair head shows. Their places and numbers are authoring choices, never a count.
The cellar's ceiling is this house's timber ground floor (the grammar's choice for this house), not the brick vault of R2's description.

The lamps' powers are hand-set in proportion to their sources (a pressure lamp of some hundreds of candlepower, a headlamp bulb without its reflector's focusing, a rag wick of about one), not calibrated.

tableaux.title: Smoke from the ground: a family dugout in a burned timber quarter

provenance.event_date_or_window: 1942-08-23/1943-02-02 (the timber quarters burned in August and September 1942; civilians lived in the ground through the winter)
provenance.place_envelope: The timber fringes of the Stalingrad city centre

sources.citation: Historical Commission interviews (Pigalyov, Vodolagin, Denisova, Ioffe), 1943-44, in Hellbeck (2015), 'The Fate of the City and Its Residents': fires not fought for want of water; people in 'shelters, basements, trenches'; children found in 'courtyards, apartments, trenches, and basements'.
sources.framing: Near-contemporary; access copy.

sources.citation: Agrafena Pozdnyakova, interview of 14 March 1943, and Hellbeck's introduction: courtyard trenches, basements, a sledge; 15,000 civilians in German-held areas at the end of November; soldiers ransacking shacks and units demolishing 'whole dwellings' for wood.
sources.framing: Named civilian witness; access copy. Her September fire (a1_burned_cellar_household) is not restaged here.

sources.citation: Beevor, Stalingrad (1998), ch. 24: children 'living in the ground for four or five winter months' (an American aid worker); a census of surviving civilians (RTsKhIDNI 17/8/226).
sources.framing: The census figure is never encoded.

sources.citation: Beevor, Stalingrad (1998), ch. 20: stovepipes 'made from empty food tins rammed together'.
sources.framing: Access copy; a practice of the pocket.

sources.citation: NAC 2-939 (Bauer, German PK), October 1942: plank-framed shelter entrances dug into a city-centre garden, one of them caved in.
sources.framing: German PK photograph; form reference.

sources.citation: Bundesarchiv Bild 183-B29644, September 1942: residents with salvaged belongings among burned wooden houses.
sources.framing: ADN caption; form reference.

documented_relationships: The timber quarters burned down to their stoves and chimneys (the grammar's burned wooden house).
Through the winter civilians lived in trenches, dugouts and cellars among them, heated by small stoves with tin stovepipes, moving goods on sledges.
Soldiers took fences and houses for firewood.
inferred_geometry_and_props: The dugout's construction and size; its floor stands at grade under a snow-covered earth mound 1.5-1.7 m high instead of a pit dug 0.5-0.7 m, because the terrain cannot be opened (brief section 7).
The choice of plot, the dugout between this plot's stove and its neighbour's, its entrance turned east out of the westerly wind.
The sledge with a sack, the bucket, the horse's lower leg and hoof on the dugout floor.
The iron bedstead in the ash, the charred sill log, the fence posts stripped of their boards.

not_shown: people, children's bodies or posed figures

host.choice: The middle of a row of five burned timber houses on the district's west fringe (block c0r3), toward the old road west; the yard gate beside it lets the dugout be seen from the lane, and its smoke rises over the chimney field.

tableaux.title: The tram that stopped on 23 August

provenance.place_envelope: A tram street of the Stalingrad city centre; the photograph is the physical reference, not the location

sources.citation: Yefim Kopyt, February 1943, Tulak Street (today Bazisnaya Street): 'a tram carcass riddled by bullets and fragments in the central part of Stalingrad', with a dead horse beside the line; Stalingrad Battle Museum-Reserve.
sources.framing: Wartime Soviet photograph; physical reference, not the location.

sources.citation: Stalingrad tram: service until 23 August 1942, the network destroyed during the battle, Kh cars from 1929, 1,524 mm gauge.
sources.framing: Local transport history.

sources.citation: Kh motor car: two axles on a 2,700 mm wheelbase, body 9,565 mm (10,270 over the couplers), 2,464 mm wide, 3,274 mm rail to roof, 12.65 t; riveted steel frame and 3 mm steel panels; roof, window frames, doors and lining of wood.
sources.framing: Vehicle data.

sources.citation: The Stalingrad trolleybus opened on 31 December 1960: no trolleybus and no twin trolley wire in 1942-43.
sources.framing: Refutes trolleybuses in 1942-43.

documented_relationships: The trams stopped when the city burned; cars stayed where they stood (network history).
By February 1943 a riddled car stood on its rails in a central street, a frozen dead horse lying in the snow beside the line (Kopyt).
inferred_geometry_and_props: The car's position and orientation on the tram street, and that this car stopped on 23 August (the network did; the photograph does not date the car).
The pattern of the fragment holes, the torn roof bays and the open door.
The collector's absence, the car's paint colour (undocumented; the prints are black and white).
The 30 m of both tracks kept clear of snow around the car (the district's tram street has no rails, L's named gap).
The half-sunk crate and bucket (as in the photograph); the fallen span wire and the knocking frame are not built.

reference_photographs.traces: tram rails flush in an earth street of the centre, October 1942
a vehicle carcass left where it stopped, capped with snow
a vanished street marked only by what stands in it
a street of the centre with fences and a pole

host.choice: A shelled four-storey block on the tram street 133 m south of the spawn, on the way to the withdrawal point: the car stands on the western track before its frontage, where the street is level across (1.6 per cent; north of the spawn the district's pads leave the street up to 11 per cent across, which would tilt a car standing on rails); 12.5 m of the street stay clear east of the car (R2: at least 6 m, so that pushing the car is the player's choice; here the car is a static obstacle, so the lane is the only way past: the ledger's tableaux row).

tableaux.title: White canopies: an air-drop canopy on a gutted block, a canister out in the open

provenance.place_envelope: Both pockets; here the German-held city centre

sources.citation: Beevor, Stalingrad (1998), ch. 22: resupply by canisters dropped by parachute; white canopies despite Sixth Army's requests for red (Winrich Behr, conversation with Beevor, 1995); men retrieving canisters in the open picked off by snipers.
sources.framing: Access copy.

sources.citation: Sgt Helmut Pist, 24th Panzer Division, interrogation 9 February 1943: air-dropped food taken by whoever found it, despite strict orders and the threat of being shot.
sources.framing: Captive context.

sources.citation: After 23 January no landings, only intermittent drops of ammunition and food (Adam and Ruhle 2015, pp. 183-189).
sources.framing: Chronology.

documented_relationships: At the end the pocket was supplied only by canisters under white canopies, and the wind carried them across the lines (Behr, Adam and Ruhle).
Men were shot trying to reach canisters in the open (Beevor ch. 22); what was found was kept by whoever found it (Pist).
inferred_geometry_and_props: The canister type (the form of photograph [05-07], not an identified model) and that there are two.
Where the canopy snagged: over the top of the last standing bay beside the collapsed end of the block.
That the split canister lies by the block's back cellar window and the unopened one 40 m out in its yard.
The low mound under snow on the far rim of the shell crater between them, 10 m short of the unopened canister, and the empty sack by it.
The line of footprints and drag marks is not built (no snow-deformation state exists for feet).

reference_photographs.traces: supply canisters of about 2.5-2.7 m lying in the snow (stencils not reproduced)
a gutted block's broken top where a canopy could catch
open snow between wall stacks, 2 February 1943
open trodden ground between ruins, 7 January 1943

not_shown: soldiers lying in the cross formation

host.choice: A five-storey block, gutted (partly collapsed: timber floors burned, a corner down), 137 m north of the spawn on the tram street: its broken south end faces the spawn, so the canopy reads on the skyline to the north of the spawn; its yard is 70 m of open snow, the canister 35 m from the nearest cover.

tableaux.title: The burned house on the courtyard: its cellar shelter and the trench beside it

provenance.event_date_or_window: 1942-09-17 (a small two-storey house on Solnechnaya Street burns with its block; the family has sheltered in its cellar, escapes through the house windows and lives in courtyard trenches afterwards)
provenance.depicted_date_or_window: 1943-01 (a later winter survival of the burned house: imagined, not the witnessed September moment)
provenance.place_envelope: The residential streets of the Stalingrad city centre; the testimony names Solnechnaya Street. This district building is not her house and no address is claimed (movable scene block, owner decision of 28 September 2026).

sources.citation: Agrafena Pozdnyakova, Historical Commission interview, 14 March 1943: the small two-storey house on Solnechnaya Street, the cellar, the courtyard trenches, the fire of 17 September, the escape through the house windows, the walls left standing.
sources.framing: Near-contemporary Soviet commission interview in an edited Russian publication; access copy. Cite Hellbeck, Stalingrad (НЛО 2015 / PublicAffairs 2015).

sources.citation: Pozdnyakova testimony, English edited edition: Hellbeck, Stalingrad: The City That Defeated the Third Reich (2015), ch. 18.
sources.framing: Edited English rendering; access copy. Cite the printed edition.

documented_relationships: The household sheltered in the cellar of its small two-storey house (Pozdnyakova).
On 17 September the house burned with its block; the family got out through the house windows; the walls survived (Pozdnyakova).
Afterwards the family sheltered in trenches dug in the courtyard (Pozdnyakova).
inferred_geometry_and_props: The house: a burned two-storey merchant house of the district, the kind the testimony describes, not her house; its cellar and stair are the grammar's.
The winter dressing: a later survival of the September fire (the scene catalog's own boundary: the September escape is not frozen as a winter tableau).
The cellar objects (an empty bench, a bucket, two plain crates, an iron bed frame carried down) and their places; none is in the testimony, none belongs to a named person.

The charred joists and lath of the burned upper floor lying on the rubble over the ground-floor vault (the vault held: nothing burned fell into the cellar), and brick fallen into the cellar's street room.

The trench: its line, 14 m long, 1.2 m wide, 0.9 m deep, beginning 2.8 m behind the back wall in line with the house's end wall and running out across the courtyard, the spoil banks along it and the stakes; the testimony gives no dimensions and no connection to the cellar, and none is built.

The props of the scene block (tools/worldgen/historical_household_20260925.py) re-seated in this building's own rooms; its table, chair and upper-floor furniture burned with the floors and are not placed.

host.choice: A burned two-storey merchant house with a cellar (the testimony's "small two-storey house"), 133 m east of the spawn across the tram street, whose back door opens onto a courtyard of open ground where the trench can be dug. Its timber upper floor and roof burned and lie as ash and rubble on the brick vault of its ground floor; the cellar under the vault is whole, reached by the stair hall's cellar stair from the street door.

tableaux.title: The cellar ward: bedding on boards and the cold ash of a fire on the floor

provenance.depicted_date_or_window: 1943-01 (the cellar's cold aftermath: an authoring choice, not the witnessed days)
provenance.place_envelope: The diary's factory cellar in the factory district by the Volga. Relocated by owner decision (28 September 2026) into the cellar of a 1930s apartment block of the city-centre district: the host is residential, not a factory, against the scene catalog's own placement rule (requires a factory cellar, forbids a domestic one); the district has no factory and no cellared workshop. Nothing here claims this building, a factory, or the diarist's distances.

sources.citation: Unnamed corporal, 10./Infanterie-Regiment 578, 305th Infantry Division, diary entries of 15-18 December 1942 (captured; Soviet translation dated 1 January 1943), Stalingrad Battle Museum-Reserve KP 25224: a factory cellar entered on the 15th; on the 16th wounded carried down into its darkness and a fire burning directly on its floor; on the 18th a wounded man carried to a doctor found, after searching, in another ruined house's cellar.
sources.framing: Unnamed author; the surviving record is a Soviet wartime translation; handwriting and translation not independently authenticated.

documented_relationships: Soldiers took shelter in a factory cellar; wounded were carried down into its darkness (KP 25224, 15-16 December).
A fire was built directly on the cellar floor (KP 25224, 16 December).
The doctor was found, after searching, in another ruined house's cellar (KP 25224, 18 December).
inferred_geometry_and_props: The host and its two cellar rooms (relocated; see the place envelope).
The bedding: mattresses on salvaged boards along the walls, the central way and the door mouths kept clear; material and count are inferred, never a census.
The fire's cold aftermath: an ash and scorch patch in a ring of loose brick with stripped timber beside it; unlit.
The single bucket as the ration vessel, the crates at the edges, the displaced planks.

The props of the scene block (tools/worldgen/historical_ward_20260925.py) re-seated in this building's rooms; the block's factory shell, steel frame and ramps are not built (the host's own walls, floor and stair bound the cellar). Its stencilled crates are replaced by the plain board crate.

reference_photographs.traces: a factory basement in use in December 1942 (the Red October calibration shop): a low vault, a lamp, a table of boards
men resting on bedding along a cellar's walls, December 1942
the factory district above such cellars, January 1943
a small fire and mess tins in a shelter

not_shown: a factory claimed for this building

host.choice: The district's cellars are all under dwellings; this shelled five-storey block keeps its concrete floors over a long cellar whose street-side rooms open into one another, the nearest to a dark industrial cellar the district has; it is 254 m from the red-cross cellar, so the two cellar stations are not read as one.

tableaux.title: Gumrak: the burned stores beside the route west

provenance.event_date_or_window: 1942-11-23/1942-11-25 (late November 1942: the entry headed 22 November and the next dated entry, 25 November)
provenance.depicted_date_or_window: 1943-01 (the cold aftermath of the fires: elapsed time an authoring choice)
provenance.place_envelope: Gumrak (the station, stores and airfield north-west of the city) as a route composite: beside the act's route west, outside the city-centre district, by owner decision of 28 September 2026; not Gumrak's plan and not at Gumrak. The separate Karpovka-road observation (deliberate burning, ready weapons) is not part of it.

sources.citation: Anonymous officer, 79th Infantry Division, diary (captured; Soviet translation), Stalingrad Battle Museum-Reserve KP 25221: in the entry headed 22 November 1942, the return journey reaches Gumrak the next morning; traffic arriving from Stalingrad; houses, food and clothing burning.
sources.framing: Wartime witness account mixed with rumour and reported orders; the exact hour is ambiguous.

documented_relationships: At Gumrak houses, food and clothing were burning when the diarist passed, the morning after 22 November 1942 (KP 25221).
Traffic was arriving from Stalingrad at the same time (KP 25221).
inferred_geometry_and_props: The store (a burned brick workshop of the district grammar) and the house across the road (a burned merchant house); their siting on the route west.

The cold aftermath: ash footprints, charred planks and roof timber, scorched and surviving crates of preserved food, scorched baggage; no cause of the fires is assigned and nothing is claimed as an ammunition depot.
The unloading group and barrels by the road and the brick fallen from the walls.

The props of the scene block (tools/worldgen/historical_gumrak_20260925.py) re-seated in the two buildings' frames. Replaced for the wordless rule: the library's tins (branded labels) by plain rusted tins, its stencilled crates by the plain board crate.

reference_photographs.traces: the pocket's road: abandoned vehicles and dropped loads along it
abandoned vehicles and their loads in the snow
a load left on the route, rime on metal
a burned railway yard of the region, October 1942

not_shown: a tank or gun claimed from the source

host.choice: A burned brick store built for the scene by the district tool (the Gumrak site, tools/worldgen/urban_intro_district.py) beside the old road, the act's route west, where it comes back to level ground 840 m from the spawn, outside the district; its burned roof lies as ash over its floor.

tableaux.title: Gumrak: the burned house across the road from the stores

provenance.event_date_or_window: 1942-11-23/1942-11-25 (late November 1942: the entry headed 22 November and the next dated entry, 25 November)
provenance.depicted_date_or_window: 1943-01 (the cold aftermath of the fires: elapsed time an authoring choice)
provenance.place_envelope: Gumrak (the station, stores and airfield north-west of the city) as a route composite: beside the act's route west, outside the city-centre district, by owner decision of 28 September 2026; not Gumrak's plan and not at Gumrak. The separate Karpovka-road observation (deliberate burning, ready weapons) is not part of it.

sources.citation: Anonymous officer, 79th Infantry Division, diary (captured; Soviet translation), Stalingrad Battle Museum-Reserve KP 25221: in the entry headed 22 November 1942, the return journey reaches Gumrak the next morning; traffic arriving from Stalingrad; houses, food and clothing burning.
sources.framing: Wartime witness account mixed with rumour and reported orders; the exact hour is ambiguous.

documented_relationships: At Gumrak houses, food and clothing were burning when the diarist passed, the morning after 22 November 1942 (KP 25221).
Traffic was arriving from Stalingrad at the same time (KP 25221).
inferred_geometry_and_props: The house (a burned one-storey merchant house built for the scene by the district tool) across the road from the store; the diary's "houses" burning are otherwise unspecified.
A cold fire scar on its floor, its roof timber fallen, a table and a chair left: restrained domestic remnants, no owner asserted.

reference_photographs.traces: the pocket's road: abandoned vehicles and dropped loads along it
abandoned vehicles and their loads in the snow
a load left on the route, rime on metal
a burned railway yard of the region, October 1942

not_shown: a tank or gun claimed from the source

host.choice: The house the district tool sets across the old road from the Gumrak store, beyond the road's poles, facing the road.
